assessment: The incumbent offers a predictable, free conversational routine with a demonstrated paper channel. Seven frequent attendees value its repetition; the concrete limiting observation is five occasional attendees struggling to enter conversations already familiar to partners. Familiarity may help continuity while hindering entry, but causation is unestablished. Slips record useful practice on 49/72 occasions and correct preparation on 48/72; only 72 slips cover 97 attendances, speaking was not timed, and responses cannot be linked across weeks. Coordination sometimes exceeds 90 minutes. Current evidence does not establish the success targets.

openings.claim: Unequal familiarity with a conversation may reduce useful practice independently of time lost choosing partners.
openings.delta: Preserve the repeated session structure while testing a shared starting point within each pair.
openings.prediction: After pairing, a brief mutual reset using a fresh opening prompt will improve occasional attendees' useful-practice reports even if pair-formation duration remains similar.
openings.probe: Within existing practice time, alternate ordinary prompts and a fresh opening prompt with equal turns. Use anonymous observation to record formation time, each partner's speaking time, and partner changes; collect useful-practice reports with optional attendance-frequency categories. Compare conditions, especially occasional attendees, over six sessions and record volunteer minutes.
assumptions: A fresh shared prompt can reduce familiarity asymmetry without public proficiency labels.
Observed speaking duration supplements, rather than replaces, participants' judgments of usefulness.

openings.claim: Confusion between current and earlier preparation instructions may contribute to incorrect task identification; missing information remains an alternative explanation.
openings.delta: Test temporal clarity of the existing paper channel before adding coordination channels.
openings.prediction: Explicit session dates and one clearly marked next task will reduce earlier-task answers; persistent blank answers would suggest a different access or comprehension problem.
openings.probe: Use existing topic sheets with explicit current and next session dates, retain paper access and optional messaging, and make spare sheets available at each session. Track earlier-task errors separately from blanks and correct answers, including optional paper-only status, across six sessions; log printing and question-answering minutes against the 90-minute ceiling.
assumptions: Readers can interpret the dates and task wording.
Changing labels requires little additional volunteer effort.
No preparation completion or attendance history becomes a condition of participation.
